newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia sets ambitious economic targets for 1997.
newsitem.headline: Colombia sets ambitious economic targets for 1997.

text.p: Colombia unveiled its economic targets for 1997 Friday, led by an ambitious forecast of 4.0 to 4.5 percent growth in the country's gross domestic product.

The targets, which also include a goal of inflation at or under 18 percent next year, were set in a statement issued by Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo and central bank chief Miguel Urrutia after a day-long meeting behind closed doors at the Banco de la Republica.

Inflation this year is expected to total more than 22 percent -- well above the government's original target of 17 percent -- and GDP growth is seen at 2.5 to 3.0 percent, according to most independent estimates.

In addition to lower inflation, the statement said the government would seek to shave $500 million off the total public sector foreign debt in 1997 and -- after a series of privatizations, details of which were not given -- limit the public sector deficit to a maximum of 1.1 percent of GDP by year-end.

Urrutia and Ocampo said a slight modification of the peso's daily floating rate exchange band and other measures would be taken to ensure the weakening of the local currency. The target was for a devaluation of anywhere between 15 and 29 percent in 1997, they said.

The government had forecast a 13.5 percent devaluation of the peso this year to help make Colombian goods more competitive abroad and to boost the value of export revenues in real peso terms. The peso has appreciated sharply since June, however, and has lost less than 3.0 percent of its value in nominal terms against the dollar so far this year.
Growth in oil exports, and an easing of the political uncertainty that rocked Colombia in 1996, is widely expected to brighten Colombia's economic outlook next year.

The outlook remains clouded, however, by uneasy ties with Washington and the threat that the administration of U.S. President Bill Clinton will move to impose punitive economic sanctions on Colombia in March as part of the U.S. government's annual drug certification process.
